title: Buick Is Still Building Sleek Sedans, Just Not for America - AOL.com
content: Buick last sold a sedan in the U.S. in 2020, when the Regal was discontinued. Since then, the brand has been selling only crossover SUVs in its home market, but things are quite different in Buick’s largest market—China. Buick currently sells four different sedans in China—Verano, Regal, Electra L7, and LaCrosse—and a fifth one will soon join their ranks. Buick is bringing back the Electra GS name in the guise of a sleek-looking plug-in hybrid sedan. Inspired by last year’s Electra GS Concept, the production model looks less striking, as it often happens when a design study reaches the production stage, but it’s still an eye-catching design. The first photos of the new Buick Electra GS come courtesy of China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (via CarNewsChina), which periodically publishes regulatory filings on upcoming automotive products. As you can see in the images, the Electra GS has a more traditional sedan shape than the 2025 concept, although the fastback roofline and smooth surfaces are still there. The plug-in hybrid sedan features slim headlights that wrap around a trim piece stretching across the front end; the element can be had either in body color or in silver. A similar trim piece is found at the rear flanked by the LED taillights and a light bar that spans the entire width of the car. Unlike the concept that featured flush door handles, the Electra GS features semi-hidden door handles to comply with the current safety legislation in China. The front bumper also has a gaping grille at the bottom, while the rear features an aggressive-looking lower bumper with two trim pieces sticking out on each side and flanking the license plate area. From a size standpoint, the Buick Electra GS measures 196 inches in length, which places it in Audi A6 territory. It’s around two inches shorter than the Electra L7, another sedan sold by Buick in China with battery electric and extended range electric powertrains. The GS is also 1.5 inches narrower and has a 5.3-inch shorter wheelbase than the L7. The Electra GS uses a plug-in hybrid powertrain consisting of either a 97-horsepower naturally aspirated 1.5-liter four-cylinder gas or a 154-hp turbocharged 1.5-liter. Each of the gas engines is paired with a front-mounted 221-hp electric motor powered by a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack. Since both the ICE and the electric motor are placed on the front axle, all Electra GS variants are front-wheel-drive-only. The more powerful variant enables a top speed of 118 miles per hour. The battery capacity is not yet available, but the filing does note that there are two different suppliers for it: Rept Battero Energy and Zenergy. Built jointly with GM’s joint-venture partner SAIC, the Electra GS will enable Buick to compete with popular models like the BYD Qin L DM-i (known as the Seal 6 in Europe) and Geely Galaxy L6 in the Chinese market. Pricing and full specifications will be announced closer to the model’s launch. Since we’re talking about a model developed and built in China with software developed specifically for Chinese consumers, it goes without saying that Buick couldn’t sell the Electra GS in the United States even if it wanted to. title: Buick’s Newest Sedan Has A GS Badge, But Isn’t For America - CarBuzz
content: Many automakers have different lineups for different regions, but one brand with arguably the most divergent lineups is Buick. In the US, we know it for upscale SUVs from subcompact to full-size, and they're all fairly conventional. You won't find any major electrification in any American Buick. Over in China, though, you can get SUVs, sedans, and even minivans with the brand, and you'll find all manner of hybridization and even full electric power. Now, Buick's Chinese division is about to get another hybrid in a sleek sedan package, and it has us wondering what's taking so long for American hybrids. This latest hybrid is another in the Electra line of cars, and it adopts the GS suffix that has long adorned Buick's highest-performance models. The brand hasn't officially introduced the model, but thanks to details being published by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, we get an early (and extremely clear) look at it. It's a clean-looking thing with a nice low nose and a fastback roofline. Close examination of the rear shows a shut line that goes around the rear glass, suggesting it's a liftback, rather than a true sedan. It also has slim wraparound LED lighting at the front and back, and the diffuser section of the rear bumper reminds us a bit of the Porsche Taycan. While svelte, the Electra GS also looks a bit anonymous, as it follows the Chinese car design trend of going basically grille-less, but also not doing much with the front and rear fascias. The documents do show optional contrasting silver panels for the front and rear that add at least a bit of visual interest. The photos also show cameras on the fenders, and a lidar sensor on the roof. These won't be standard, though. Other images show roof and fender designs without driver assist components. Because of all the specifications included in the government documents, we also know how big the Electra GS is. It's 196 inches long, and it has a wheelbase of 112.8 inches. It's almost identical in size to the Toyota Crown, though its a little more than an inch shorter than Toyota's tall sedan. Despite the name, the Electra GS won't be much of a sports sedan. The documents show that it will be a plug-in hybrid, and at least one version of the car will feature a turbocharged 1.5-liter four-cylinder making 154 horsepower. It should also make 170 pound-feet of torque assuming it's the same engine that's used in the Electra E7 SUV. The electric motor is gutsier, making 221 horsepower, and, assuming the E7 connection, 243 pound-feet of torque. On the E7, Buick lists combined power and torque, but it simply adds the peak numbers together, which doesn't necessarily give an accurate picture of just how much propulsive power is provided. We would assume combined power is somewhere near the electric motor's output. It's adequate, but far from exhilarating. CarScoops reports that a base model will also be available with the lower-output powertrain from the E7. It uses a naturally-aspirated 1.5-liter four-cylinder making 97 hp and 96 pound-feet of torque. In the E7, that engine is still paired with the same 221-hp electric motor. Being a plug-in hybrid, the Electra GS will be able to charge up from the grid and operate fully electrically. Assuming that the powertrains are taken directly from the E7, it should get the same 32.6-kWh battery pack as the SUV. On China's test loop, that provides 146 miles of range. That would absolutely be lower on the US test cycle, but that's still a sizable battery and would likely provide plenty of range. The GS will probably go even further on a charge thanks to being more aerodynamic. Just like every other Chinese Buick, with the sole exception of the Envision, it's all but guaranteed the Electra GS won't come to America. Tariffs on Chinese vehicles, plus the cost of safety and emissions certification, on top of being a less-than-popular body style in our market make it a non-starter. Although it's possible it could show up in other markets, maybe even as close as Mexico, since Buick is looking to bring more of its Chinese models to other markets. The fact that Buick has added another hybrid to its already extensive roster does raise the question of what's taking so long for GM to bring hybrids back to the US. Emissions certification and production locations would be the main hindrances, just as it would be for a complete vehicle. GM does have hybrid plans for the US, though, as it's pouring money into a Michigan facility to build hybrid powertrains in the next few years, likely for its full-size SUVs that could include Buick's own Enclave. title: BMW F 450 GS Sport Launched At Rs 5.90 Lakh - DriveSpark
content: The BMW F 450 GS Sport has been launched in India at Rs 5.90 lakh (ex-showroom). The F 450 GS Sport is the fourth variant of the middleweight adventure motorcycle from BMW Motorrad and it comes with Sport Suspension and an exclusive Racing Red finish. Until now, the F 450 GS was sold in Base, Exclusive and GS Trophy variants. The new Sport slots in between the Exclusive and the GS Trophy, and is Rs 25,000 more affordable than the top-spec Trophy variant. When the BMW F 450 GS first went on sale in April, the Base was priced at Rs 4.70 lakh, the Exclusive at Rs 4.90 lakh and the GS Trophy at Rs 5.30 lakh. Prices have gone up since, and the range now starts at Rs 5.35 lakh. (All figures mentioned are ex-showroom). The new BMW F 450 GS Sport variant uses the same 420cc liquid-cooled parallel-twin as the rest of the range. The engine pushes out 48bhp at 8,750rpm and 43Nm at 6,750rpm through a 6-speed gearbox. BMW quotes an unladen weight of 178kg and a seat height of 845mm for the F 450 GS. Sport Suspension is the headline change in the BMW F 450 GS Sport, giving the ew variant a more focused setup than the standard Base and Exclusive variants. Gear Shift Assistant Pro is also standard, allowing clutchless gear changes under the right conditions. Riding Modes Pro adds an Enduro Pro setting to the existing Rain, Road and Enduro modes. Both the Sport and the GS Trophy get Sport Suspension and Riding Modes Pro. The Trophy adds BMW's Easy Ride Clutch, which isn't listed for the Sport, so the BMW F 450 GS Sport relies on a conventional clutch backed by Gear Shift Assistant Pro. The Trophy also has an aluminium engine guard and a tinted Rallye windscreen. With the arrival of the BMW F 450 GS Sport riders who wanted the Trophy's equipment without the Easy Ride Clutch now have that option. Racing Red paint is exclusive to the Sport. The X-shaped LED headlamp, front beak and upright proportions carry over from the other variants. title: Construction Sites Prepare for Winter… Checking Equipment-Tip-Over Risks and Replacing Cold-Weather Gear - 더글로벌기빙뉴스
content: With winter approaching, construction companies are reviewing job-site safety and working conditions. IPARK Hyundai Development (CEO Jung Kyung-gu) inspected measures at its construction site in Gimhae, South Gyeongsang Province, to address the risk of equipment tipping over as the ground freezes and thaws, as well as icy conditions along worker routes. GS E&C (CEO Heo Yun-hong) is updating its site workwear with warmth and ease of movement in mind, and will distribute fall/winter jackets and winter parkas in phases. According to announcements from the two companies on the 6th, IPARK Hyundai Development CEO Jung Kyung-gu, Chief Safety Officer (CSO) Yang Seung-cheol and other executives visited the Gimhae Urban Planning Facility civil engineering project site and the Gimhae Sinmun Central IPARK site in succession on the 5th. GS E&C has introduced three new types of site workwear: spring/fall jackets, fall/winter jackets and winter parkas. At the Gimhae Sinmun Central IPARK site, where workers are driving piles and installing retaining walls, the executives checked measures to prevent equipment from tipping over due to ground freezing and thawing. They also checked whether safe routes had been secured to prevent workers from slipping when the ground freezes. At the Gimhae Urban Planning Facility site, which is nearing completion, they reviewed the terrain, landscaping layout and road paving. CEO Jung stressed the need to identify potential hazards at each stage of construction in advance and prepare for them, from the start of a project through its completion. GS E&C has completed distribution of the spring/fall jackets and plans to distribute the fall/winter jackets and winter parkas in turn. The company held surveys and review sessions to select the new workwear, and about 2,000 employees took part in a vote on jacket design preferences. At year-end, it plans to survey employees on warmth, ease of movement and ease of washing and care, and use the results in decisions on additional production and future designs. Workwear in good condition will be reused. The company is considering processing unusable inventory and used workwear collected from sites in the future into recycled fiber panels for furniture and interior finishing materials. GS E&C is also exploring ways to use the material to improve the environments of its “Dream and Hope Study Rooms” and school after-school care classrooms. title: Assam Sahitya Sabha poll: Race for VP, GS posts gathers pace as form collection ends - The Assam Tribune
content: Saturday was the last date for collecting nomination forms following the issuance of the election notification. Jorhat, Nov 7: The Assam Sahitya Sabha’s central office in Jorhat saw heightened activity on Saturday as aspirants collected nomination papers for the posts of vice-president and general secretary for the 2027-29 term. Saturday was the last date for collecting nomination forms following the issuance of the election notification. As of the time of filing this report, Dr Bipin Chandra Kalita and Jadav Chandra Sarma had collected nomination papers for the post of vice-president. “Another candidate, Ajay Singha, has arrived, but I am yet to know which post he intends to contest. We are expecting four to five more people to come and collect nomination forms,” said Achyut Senapati, secretary of the Assam Sahitya Sabha. For the post of general secretary, Nayanmoni Choudhury, Dr Sanjib Kumar Sarma and Dr Sahir Bhuyan had collected nomination forms. The number of aspirants was expected to rise by the evening. Sarma said he was considering contesting for the general secretary’s post. He is an English teacher at Dispur College and currently serves as secretary of the Sabha’s Guwahati office. “I have been associated with the Sabha for a long time, and the experience I have gained through this association will help me take the organisation forward,” Sarma said. According to the election schedule, candidates will submit their nomination papers to the Election Committee at the Assam Sahitya Sabha’s Guwahati office on November 9 and 10, between 11 am and 2 pm. Scrutiny of the nomination papers will be conducted on November 11 and 12. Candidates seeking to withdraw their nominations may do so at the Sabha’s Guwahati office between 11 am and 3 pm on the prescribed dates. The final list of candidates for the posts of vice-president and general secretary will be published on November 13. Ballot papers for voting at the district and branch levels will be distributed between November 17 and 20. Voting will then be held at district and branch Sahitya Sabhas from November 21 to December 4. The election process is expected to determine the leadership of the Assam Sahitya Sabha for the 2027-29 term, with the number of contenders for the two key posts likely to become clearer after nomination and scrutiny.

title: The US Midterms: Reshaping the Stock Market - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The US midterm elections could strengthen the stock market rotation that was already underway, says Lou Miller, global head of Custom Basket Trading in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. Traditional defensive sectors such as consumer staples are expensive right now, but healthcare stocks may provide defense along with earnings acceleration, Miller explains on The Markets podcast. He also says that stocks related to the data-center buildout have fallen sharply, resetting valuations and lowering the bar for positive surprises. Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, November 5th, and we're here on the Goldman Sachs trading floor with Lou Miller, who is our global head of our custom baskets business within FICC and Equities. And on the back of the midterm elections, we're going to explore the market reaction and where we go from here. Chris Hussey: Let's start with the rotation trade that you can see from your baskets group. In particular, that there was a rotation already happening before the midterms. How is that evolving post midterms? Where do you think it heads into the year end? Lou Miller: Yeah, so we've seen, especially in the second half of the year, it's been a really challenging environment for active investors, and we've seen people get very defensive. If you look at beta-adjusted net exposure in our prime book, it's definitely at very low levels versus history. Chris Hussey: Let me peel back the onion a little bit on the rotation. Let's talk about data centers if we can. How is that data center trade holding up in the post-election world? Lou Miller: Worse than I would've thought. I think it's bigger picture concerns like ROI, open-source competition, limits on capital markets came into picture the last few months. The AI data center trade, the right tail of that trade has increasingly gotten removed, and multiples have dramatically dropped to much healthier levels. We now see data center stocks down 36% from their highs earlier this year. And then some of the higher beta areas like memory down 42%, optical networking down 46%, even NeoCloud's down 57%. So the early reaction was way more extreme than I would've expected, but I think the silver lining is the bar is much, much lower for surprises and there are positive catalysts ahead. Think about this: the multiple for the data center trade is about half of what it was in June. We're at liberation day lows in terms of multiples. So you can't argue valuation is a headwind anymore, and there are some positive catalysts ahead. Chris Hussey: Okay. I want to dive now into a little bit of a comment you made about defensives, and I want to go back to the post-pandemic era where tech became the new defensives. Let's explore the AI trade more broadly. You talked about a rotation. You talked about the data center trade. What about the AI trade more broadly? Is that a new defensive kind of trade, or is that really evolving? Lou Miller: I think the next leg of the AI trade is actually healthcare, and I think that's also a very defensive sector that historically is very uncorrelated to AI. Healthcare, we notice those companies are getting very involved at, like, the tools and diagnostics level and that there's now we're going from headwinds to tailwinds there. There's both cyclical and secular drivers there and it's really one of the few sectors that we're going to see accelerating growth next year. AI touches a lot of different parts of the economy, a lot of different parts of the market everything from the application layer, like cybersecurity, but I think healthcare is an area that increasingly looks more and more credible. Chris Hussey: All right. If the new defensives aren't the new defensive, what is the new defensive? What do you want to play defense? Lou Miller: So yeah. So expensive defensives I don't think are defensive. Lou Miller: In a slowing growth environment, not just for the AI CapEx complex, but the real economy it does make sense to be defensive, but you don't want to take it too far. You don't want to bury your head in the sand. So you take staples, for example, the earnings yield of staples is half of the high yield bond yield. The dividend yield of staples is half of the 10-year treasury yield. To me, that's not a good deal for investors. I think people should look beyond the traditional defensive label and look for other characteristics, like quality or free cash flow yield or earnings yield in this higher nominal growth backdrop. I think those dynamics are going to be a lot more defensive than a traditional defensive like staples. Chris Hussey: All right, great. So, we've walked through it. We've walked through the AI trade, the data center trade, the expensive defensives. Let's put a bow on it. What's the trade? Lou Miller: I think the S&P 500 excluding AI is the trade. So rather than pay 25 times earnings for some, you know, boring consumer product, you can pay a high teen multiple for low teens earnings growth. These are some of the highest quality balance sheets in the market. You're buying quality compounders in a decelerating growth environment. That seems like a safe play here over the next six months. Chris Hussey: I'm just curious, if you buy the S&P ex AI, how many stocks is that? Lou Miller: Well, you can, you can get about 500 if you- Just got to add a few extra. Chris Hussey: I like that. I love that. All right. As we go deeper into the end of the year, what are you watching for? Lou Miller: Employment, inflation, the geopolitical events that have passed, and then the rest of earnings season. Those are key. And then longer term, I'm watching the equity capital markets quite closely, debt capital markets closely, and then the FOMC decision on December 9th. Chris Hussey: I know it's early yet, but I've already gotten some Hallmark ads in front of me. Chris Hussey: Oh, a relaxed Santa Rally. I like myself a relaxed Santa. Lou, thanks so much for joining us. Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening. title: Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Jan Hatzius Joins CNBC to Discuss the US Jobs Report and the Economic Outlook - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The recent stronger-than-expected employment report indicates a stable labor market, according to Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Jan Hatzius. He joined CNBC to discuss his views on the data and his outlook for the year ahead. Host: Welcome back. The October jobs number came in hotter than expected: nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000, above nearly every forecast. Joining us is Jan Hatzius, Goldman Sachs Chief Economist, to discuss the report, the midterms, markets, data centers, and more. Jan, it is great to have you. Host: There is nothing wrong with this number, I assume you agree. Do you think it marks the beginning of something new? Jan Hatzius: Definitely nothing wrong with it. It is a very solid report, certainly as far as payrolls are concerned. There is some month-to-month volatility, but we think the underlying trend in job growth is probably back above 100,000. That is more solid than it was earlier in the year. What we are not seeing is sustained downward pressure on the unemployment rate. It edged down a little, but it has remained in the 4.1% to 4.2% range. To me, this still looks like a labor market that is stable at about full employment. We think it will probably stay roughly in that range over time, which remains consistent with relatively subdued wage growth and low inflation. Host: How low can claims get? Are we scraping the bottom of that historic range? Jan Hatzius: It is the lowest we have seen in a series that goes back more than five decades. Layoffs are at extremely low levels, which is consistent with what we see in other indicators. Hiring continues to be relatively subdued as well, so we have not really seen a major pickup in hiring. It is still a more stagnant environment, but at a very solid level. Host: The markets this week have been rethinking the possibility of a more elongated buildout cycle. Does that lead you to lower your nominal GDP estimates for next year? Jan Hatzius: We are growing at a very rapid pace right now. GDP numbers fluctuate, but we are talking about growth with a three-handle in the second and third quarters, and likely in the fourth quarter as well. I do think growth will be softer next year. We have thought that before, but we have not made a change to our underlying growth estimate. We think it is probably in the 2% to 2.5% range, which should keep the unemployment rate roughly stable. There are some downside risks to that growth outlook. We have seen tightening in financial conditions of about 50 basis points according to our index. There are also questions around energy prices, the war with Iran and its implications for real income growth, as well as the AI buildout and its effects on both GDP and the labor market. Host: Goldman also closely monitors increases in enterprise efficiency from AI use, or at least expected productivity gains. Where are we now, and what are your expectations for 2027? Jan Hatzius: We have seen some effects on the labor market, mainly in the technology sector. That has been worth roughly 10,000 to 15,000 fewer jobs per month in employment growth. There are some indications that this is broadening into the service sector. For example, we have begun to see a correlation across service-sector industries between employment growth and unemployment rates on one hand, and AI adoption on the other. But the relationship is still not particularly strong, and you would not expect it to be if you looked at overall labor-market outcomes. Over the next year or two, I think that relationship will probably strengthen. By 2028, it is likely to become somewhat more of a headwind for employment growth. I have a fair amount of conviction that AI will be more of a macroeconomic story by 2027, though the timing remains one of the open questions. Jan Hatzius: Yes, although at the moment it is clearly still a tailwind. Once we get into 2028, you would expect the volume of investment to flatten out, and eventually investment spending will come down. That is what tends to happen in historical investment booms: infrastructure is built out, the necessary capital stock is achieved, and investment then begins to decline. That is probably still some way off, but there is, of course, substantial uncertainty around the path. Host: We are glad we will have you around for 2027 and 2028. I hope we will speak many times. title: BMW F 450 GS Sport Variant Launch Price Rs 5.90 Lakh - RushLane
content: At the time of its launch in India, the BMW F 450 GS was offered in three variants – Base, Exclusive and GS Trophy. BMW has now introduced a new Sport variant, positioned just below the top-spec GS Trophy variant. Priced at Rs 5.90 lakh, the new F 450 GS Sport variant is Rs 35,000 costlier than the Exclusive variant and Rs 25,000 more affordable than the GS Trophy variant. BMW has also expanded the broader 450 lineup with the F 450 R roadster and the F 450 RR faired versions. BMW is offering the F 450 GS Sport variant in an exclusive Racing Red colour option. This colourway predominantly combines shades of dark red and black, along with white and grey. With this new colour, the bike is now available with three colour options. The base and Exclusive variants are available in Cosmic Black colour. The GS Trophy variant is available in Racing Blue Metallic colour. F 450 GS Sport is essentially the GS Trophy, without the Easy Ride Clutch (ERC), which is available exclusively with the GS Trophy variant. Among enthusiasts planning to buy the BMW F 450 GS, the priorities can be broadly classified into ‘with ERC’ and ‘without ERC’. For the latter group, the new Sport variant ensures that all other features are accessible including the adjustable suspension. Sport variant’s Racing Red paintwork creates an exciting contrast and complements the bike’s sporty profile. Sharp design elements of the bike are better accentuated with this new colourway. The red shade is used largely across the front cowl, fuel tank and rear side panels. Rest of the surfaces are mostly black. The Sport variant also has distinctive graphics, combining themes in white and black. This paintwork also does a good job at accommodating the gold-finished USD forks. Coming to equipment, the new Sport variant of BMW F 450 GS has sport suspension, Gear Shift Assistant Pro, offroad footrests, clear windshield and hand protection. title: The Adventure Bike That Makes Owning One Motorcycle A Boss Move - Top Speed
content: Motorcycle marketing often promotes the belief that true versatility demands a multi-bike stable: a light thumper for trails, a midweight twin for commuting, and a heavy rig for touring. Managing multiple registrations, insurance policies, and maintenance schedules turns that ideal into an expensive burden. Yet experienced riders know extreme specialization often sacrifices basic usability. Sitting quietly at the premium end of the adventure segment is an understated machine commanding a devoted following because it handles city traffic, cross-country highway miles, and backcountry gravel roads with equal poise, rendering a multi-bike garage unnecessary. The modern full-size adventure segment suffers from a chronic identity crisis, caught between desert-rally marketing and the tarmac reality of long-distance touring. To substantiate rugged off-road claims, manufacturers fit long-travel suspension and 21-inch front wheels to platforms that spend 90 percent of their lives on pavement. On asphalt, that geometry yields vague front-end feedback, slow steering, and crosswind instability. Simultaneously, taming these tall chassis at highway speeds requires massive curb weight and invasive electronics to mask the packaging compromises. Riders face an irritating trade-off: machines too detached and wallowy for spirited cornering, yet far too heavy and intimidating for low-speed technical terrain. Solving this dynamic compromise requires packaging substantial displacement without saddling the motorcycle with a tall roll center. This top-heavy pendulum effect is common to tall V-twin and inline adventure platforms. Placing heavy components as close to the ground as possible dramatically reduces turning inertia. BMW mastered this specific physical balance through its horizontally opposed boxer twin. By positioning the cylinder heads flat and low, BMW drops the core mass beneath knee level, delivering light low-speed handling, straight-line stability on washboard roads, and fatigue-free highway touring. The BMW R 1300 GS gets respect everywhere it goes, because it proves why smart mechanical packaging eliminates the need for separate motorcycles. Combining an ultra-compact boxer layout, under-engine gearbox, and low-slung chassis,it replaces three specialized machines with one integrated platform all for a base price of $20,395. With the optional automatic gearbox, the price climbs to over $25,000, but it manages to be fatigue-free even in traffic. It strips away top-heavy intimidation while retaining all-day touring comfort, establishing itself as the definitive one-bike solution. BMW's 1,300 cc engine looks to be on track to be one of the greats, with its German engineering mastery. It has liquid cooling, four valves per cylinder, BMW ShiftCam on the intake valves that changes both timing and lift, an extremely short stroke design, and a high compression ratio of 13.3:1. It generates 145 horsepower at 7,750 RPM and 110 pound-feet at 6,500 RPM, and it has a six-speed manual transmission with an assist-and-slipper clutch. A two-way quickshifter is optional, but the automated manual gearbox (also optional) is what makes it a genuinely great all-round motorcycle. A driveshaft sends power to the rear wheel, which is great for low-maintenance operation. Unlike its competitors, the R 1300 GS uses a unique chassis. This is a pressed-steel monocoque that uses the engine as a stressed member, and the subframe is bolted on. It uses the Evo Telelever wishbone front suspension that offers 7.5 inches of travel and the Paralever central monoshock at the rear with a single-sided swingarm that offers 7.9 inches of travel. Twin 310 mm floating brake discs do duty up front with radial four-piston calipers, and a 285 mm disc at the rear with a two-piston floating caliper. These are mounted on alloy wheels — a 19-inch up front and a 17-inch at the rear — with radial tubeless tires. Tubeless wire-spoke rims are an option, as are more aggressive off-road tires, so you can configure it to feel right at home on any road. The R 1300 GS is a full-size adventure motorcycle, at 87.1 inches long and 39.4 inches wide with a 59.8-inch wheelbase. The seat height is standard for the class at 33.4 inches, and it has a wet weight of 523 pounds. The fuel tank is pretty large even on the regular GS at five gallons; however, with the weight placed down low, it feels a lot lighter than it is, and this feeling is helped by the electronic suspension as well. The features list is packed with everything you would possibly want from a luxury adventure motorcycle. Hop on, and the first thing you will see is the 6.5-inch TFT instrument cluster that has Bluetooth and navigation as standard. The electronics are comprehensive as well, with a by-wire throttle and a six-axis IMU. Of course, you get ride modes, cornering ABS, traction control, and engine brake control, but the optional extras are what truly elevate the big GS. The optional DSA suspension offers automatic damping control, and you can change the rear preload at the touch of a button. This is also one of the few motorcycles that self-levels with a change in load, and the electronic suspension automatically lowers at walking speeds to make it easier to handle. BMW offers different packages for these upgrades, so you will have to check whether the feature you want is available as a standalone one or as part of a package. Be aware that the packages are quite expensive and will easily drive the price to nearly $30,000. This is the sole thing that works against the GS: the high acquisition cost. title: ADVENTURE | BMW R 1300 GS PURE - ADB Magazine
content:
There are worse ways to conduct a motorcycle debrief than sitting outside a café with a coffee and a curry pie. Jeremy Cowley had just returned from three solid days of interstate riding aboard BMW’s R 1300 GS Pure, so rather than ask him to sit down and type 2000 words about it, I figured I’d shout him lunch and hit record. Besides, after that many kilometres aboard BMW’s big boxer, his arse had probably spent enough time sitting down. Plus, do you know how hard it is for a journo to get his wallet out! Cowley is becoming our resident adventure-bike tragic whether he likes the title or not. He owns a Husqvarna Norden 901 and a 2006 KTM 950 Super Enduro, has ridden everything from the Royal Enfield Himalayan and Honda CRF300 Rally to the CFMOTO 450MT-X, and there’s plenty more big-bore ADV experience in the family. His old man has owned a Triumph Tiger 800 and now has a Tiger 1200. The GS Pure is an interesting proposition. This isn’t the fully loaded, everything-and-the-kitchen-sink GS most people picture when they hear BMW. It’s the stripped-back entry point into the R 1300 GS family, but it still gets the 1300cc ShiftCam boxer producing a whopping 107kW and 149Nm, along with electronic suspension adjustment, riding modes, a quickshifter, TFT display, keyless ignition and laced wheels. In other words, ‘Pure’ doesn’t exactly mean you’re starting the bloody thing with a kickstarter. So, with coffee in hand and the curry pie rapidly disappearing, I started with the obvious question. JEREMY: Big. And weird. I’ve never really spent much time on BMWs before, so the first thing I noticed was that motor hanging out either side. I’m a massive boxer fan from driving and racing Subarus, so I understand the concept and actually love that engine configuration, but on a motorcycle it’s strange when you’re not used to it. Normally you look down on an adventure bike and see a tank or dual tanks, but on the BMW you look down and there are two bloody cylinder heads sticking out the sides. Once you’re on it, though, it immediately feels like a nice motorcycle. Sometimes with a base-model bike you can tell where the manufacturer has saved money with maybe cheaper bars, slightly ordinary ergonomics or something that makes it feel like the povo-pack version but I didn’t really get that from the Pure. The riding position was comfortable, everything felt quality and after three big days aboard it, I wasn’t looking for an excuse to throw it in a ditch. JEREMY: Bugger me. There is just so much power. It’s that huge wave of torque where you can be cruising along in fourth gear, decide you want to disappear and it just motors. I’ve ridden some seriously fast big adventure bikes now and, for me, the power delivery from this thing was better than any of them. On the road it was beautiful, and I honestly reckon I could ride that thing around Australia. Long highway days, big open roads and huge distances are where that engine makes complete sense because you’ve always got this ridiculous amount of effortless power sitting underneath you. But I reckon it’s almost too much off-road. You’ve got 145 horsepower in an adventure bike and at some point you’ve got to ask yourself what the hell you’re supposed to do with all of it. Nobody needs that much horsepower on a dirt road. Nobody. JEREMY:  I reckon the definition of an adventure bike has changed. On the dirt, I felt like I was having to work for it more than I wanted to. That’s not because the GS is bad; it’s because it’s a massive, hugely powerful motorcycle and this particular Pure isn’t really set up to be a hardcore off-road weapon. It still has plenty of technology to make it manageable, but if I wanted to get serious in the dirt I’d start with tyres and then probably look at the suspension to get it working a little better for that sort of riding. But I don’t think that’s what this bike is trying to be. We’re talking big gravel roads, corrugations, fire trails and stuff where you’re travelling rather than trying to find the nastiest singletrack possible. Put some decent tyres on it and I’d happily point it down that sort of road all day. MITCH: Like a lounge chair you can take down the Oodnadatta Track? JEREMY: Exactly. A really bloody fast lounge chair. JEREMY: No. That boxer engine looks enormous because you’ve got those cylinders hanging out the sides, but all that weight is sitting low. Once the bike is moving it feels much lighter than you’d expect, and when you’re flowing along a road it disguises its size incredibly well. It was probably the nicest adventure-roadie-tourer-whatever-you-want-to-call-it I’ve ridden on the highway. The front-end was another thing. It’s BMW’s Telelever setup and apparently I’m supposed to have some grand opinion on that. Honestly, I didn’t. I probably wouldn’t have mentioned it because there was nothing strange about the way it behaved – it just worked. JEREMY: Fine. The rider triangle felt good sitting or standing and I never really had an ergonomic issue with it. Wind protection was decent too. It’s nowhere near the worst adventure bike I’ve ridden for buffeting although you could fit a bigger screen if you were doing huge touring kilometres. The Pure doesn’t have that giant touring screen, but again, that’s part of what this model is. The only thing that annoyed me was BMW’s scroll-wheel controller on the left grip. I’m not a fan of those systems on bikes generally, so it’s not really a BMW-specific whinge. It works, I just reckon there are simpler ways of doing it. MITCH: ARE BIG-BORE ADVENTURE BIKES BECOMING TOURERS? JEREMY: I think once you get into the 1200 and 1300cc stuff now, you’re really moving towards touring. Look at the bikes around 900cc, you can ride those things all day on the road without a drama, but they’re still bloody capable when you get properly off-road. My KTM 950 Super Enduro is a 2006 model and the 950/990 generation is still regarded by plenty of people as some of the best adventure bikes KTM ever made. It’s funny because the market spent years moving towards 1200 and 1300cc bikes, and now we’re almost coming back around to that 900-ish capacity because it’s such a good compromise. JEREMY: Tyres first, depending on what I was doing. My 950 has a proper aggressive off-road tyre because when I use that bike it’s generally at an event where I know I’m going into the dirt. My Norden 901 has more of a 70/30 tyre because I actually ride it on the road to get places, and when I hit the dirt I’ll drop a couple of psi and get on with it. That’s probably exactly how I’d approach the BMW. If you’re doing 70 per cent bitumen to get to 30 per cent dirt, there’s no point fitting a massive aggressive knob and destroying it at highway speeds before you’ve even reached the fun stuff. The sort of person buying a GS in Sydney, Melbourne or Canberra is probably going to spend a fair chunk of every adventure just getting out of town. JEREMY: Yep. The Pure has Eco, Rain, Road and Enduro modes, and Rain mode is actually really nice on the dirt. It takes the edge off the throttle and gives you some slip without letting the thing completely light up, which isn’t a bad idea when you’ve got a 1300cc boxer trying to fire you at the horizon. Dad used Rain mode quite a bit and I can understand why. A lot of adventure riders do the same thing. You don’t necessarily need maximum aggression just because you’ve left the bitumen; sometimes making a huge motorcycle softer and easier to manage actually lets you ride it faster and with less effort. And that, really, is where we landed once the coffees were empty and Cowley had demolished the pie. The R 1300 GS Pure isn’t pretending to be a 1300cc enduro bike, and perhaps we’ve reached the point where we need to stop expecting enormous adventure motorcycles to be one. title: Global Music Revenues Are Forecast to Rise as Subscriber Growth Beats Expectations - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Global music industry revenues are expected to reach approximately $200 billion annually by 2035 amid an improving outlook for subscription streaming. New subscription models, AI, and direct-to-consumer offerings are creating opportunities for the industry to reach audiences in new ways, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The music market undershot growth expectations over the last several years. The new forecast represents the first time in three years that Goldman Sachs Research has raised its long-term outlook for the industry, Stephen Laszczyk and Eric Sheridan write in the team’s 2026 edition of the annual “Music in the Air” report. Goldman Sachs Research expects global music revenues to increase at 6.7% year-on-year in 2026 and at a compound rate of 5.8% per year between 2025 and 2035. “While growth is likely to moderate from the pace observed during the industry's streaming adoption phase, we continue to see a long runway for industry expansion supported by favorable consumer behavior and an increasingly diversified monetization model,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write. Music streaming subscriptions are growing faster than expected Paid streaming subscriptions are helping to shore up the outlook for recorded music. After three consecutive downgrades to its forecast for 2030 recorded music revenues, Goldman Sachs Research’s outlook for the segment this year reflects improvements in streaming revenue, physical revenue, and download and other digital revenue. Subscription streaming revenue is growing faster, mainly because subscriber numbers are increasing more quickly than expected and revenue per user is rising in developed markets. Our analysts are factoring in more consistent price increases from streaming platforms as music labels increasingly incorporate higher royalties into their contracts and streaming platforms introduce new premium service tiers. At the same time, increasing fan demand for vinyl and CDs is helping lift the outlook for physical music revenues in markets like Japan, South Korea, and the US. “We expect these trends to continue as fans increasingly view physical formats as collectibles rather than as a way to listen, and as artists incorporate physical formats into their album rollouts and tour experiences,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write. Paid subscription streaming revenue beat our analysts’ expectations in 2025, and Goldman Sachs Research expects further growth ahead, driven by emerging markets. Laszczyk and Sheridan forecast the percentage of internet users with paid streaming subscriptions in emerging markets to rise from 10% in 2025 to 15% in 2035, with subscriber numbers boosted by growing populations and increasing internet penetration. Paid subscriptions in developed markets also have room to grow, according to Laszczyk and Sheridan, who expect the number of paid subscribers in the US, Canada, Europe, and Australasia to rise to 568 million in 2035 from 398 million in 2025. Only around 53% of Americans subscribed to paid music streaming in 2025, compared with around 60% for gaming and 90% for on-demand video. Goldman Sachs Research expects most developed markets to approach peak penetration for paid music streaming at 60% by 2035. Older age groups and new products could help drive paid music users Older listeners could be an untapped audience. Data from the UK shows that older listeners are less likely to use paid streaming and less likely to convert from free to paid users. “We see opportunity for increased conversion from free to paid among older age groups, especially as younger age cohorts who are heavy users of paid streaming services grow older, and as streaming providers adapt their marketing strategies to target older demographics,” Laszczyk and Sheridan write. Introducing an ad-light tier could also help streaming providers drive subscriber acquisition. Goldman Sachs Research estimates that a small incremental fee of around $1-2 per month for a reduced advertising load could result in subscriber growth. “This follows a similar playbook to what has already been implemented in video streaming,” Laszczyk and Sheridan observe. If 10% of free streaming users in developed markets shifted to a $1 ad-light tier, global ad-supported revenues would rise by around 8%, Goldman Sachs Research estimates. Another emerging opportunity in streaming is direct-to-consumer offerings, where artists build a direct relationship with their fans without an intermediary platform controlling access to that audience. This innovation is still in its early stages, Laszczyk and Sheridan write. But “if this ecosystem continues to develop the way it has been, the direct-to-consumer opportunity could grow from representing tens of millions of dollars of revenue today to hundreds of millions over the next decade.” Increased touring and new venues are buoying live music Despite pressure on consumer wallets from tariffs, gasoline prices, and higher interest rates, our analysts expect the market for live music to grow 6% in 2026, driven by a strong global arena and stadium business. This supports Goldman Sachs Research’s thesis that demand for live events has increased globally since the Covid-19 pandemic, and that the sector is less exposed to economic downturns than other forms of discretionary spending. Looking ahead, our analysts expect live music to grow at a similar 6% compound rate through 2035, underpinned by an increasing supply of diverse and popular artists touring over the next decade. Stronger financial incentives to tour and efforts by record labels to promote new talent are set to drive the live music sector, Laszczyk and Sheridan project. And they expect venue capacity to grow, with operators poised to open several dozen new music venues around the world in the next five to seven years. AI’s impact on the music industry has been “the biggest debate among music investors over the last year,” Laszczyk and Sheridan say. One concern is that AI-generated music will displace human artists, but Laszczyk and Sheridan believe that fear is overblown for higher-profile artists in the near term. While the team does see some potential for cannibalization by AI over the long term, they expect that it will mostly be limited to lower-value music (including background and study music as well as mid-tier artists). Only a mid-single-digit percentage of consumers used an AI music generation tool at least monthly as of the fourth quarter of 2025. As of the third quarter of 2025, around 55% of music creators had used an AI tool in the past year, but mostly for production workflow or mastering rather than to generate entirely new songs. At the same time, AI represents an opportunity for music labels and rights holders: Streaming providers and tech companies can use the technology to personalize recommendations, curate content, and turn passive listeners into active creators. “We believe that monetization will ultimately make its way back to the rights holders in a way that we think will disproportionately benefit some of these higher-end artists where AI music is likely created off of their image and likeness, their melodies, or their lyrics, given how popular they are,” Laszczyk says. title: Buick Electra Leaks Online: This Is What You're Missing, America! - autoevolution
content:
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) has leaked the official product images and filing data for the upcoming Buick Electra GS plug-in hybrid sedan. Developed by the SAIC-GM joint venture, the large, fastback-style sedan is tailored specifically for the Chinese market and is very unlikely to ever set wheels on American land due to regulatory hurdles and prohibitive tariffs. The production version represents a significant departure from the much taller, hatchback-like Electra GS Concept that made its debut in April 2025 as a preview of a future production model. And this is it! It may not be the concept car’s identical twin, but it is the next best thing. With styling that pays tribute to Buick’s iconic Gran Sport lineup, the Electra GS PHEV car features ultra-slim, C-shaped LED headlights linked by an LED strip. The Buick tri-shield logo sits right below on a less aggressive "shark-nose" front fascia. The Electra GS is the slightly shorter and potentially more affordable alternative to Buick’s existing Electra L7 Sportback sedan. It measures 190.0 inches (4,980 millimeters) in length, 75.4 inches (1,915 millimeters) in width, and 58.9 inches (1,495 millimeters) in height, sitting on a wheelbase of 112.8 inches (2,865 millimeters). Those numbers make it slightly smaller than the Buick Electra L7. The leaked documents confirm the plug-in hybrid setup, which combines the electric motor, good for 221 horsepower (224 metric horsepower), with either the naturally aspirated 1.5-liter or the turbocharged 1.5-liter inline-four. The naturally aspirated engine produces 72 horsepower (73 metric horsepower, while the turbocharged unit churns out 154 horsepower (156 metric horsepower). The base variant rolls off the production line with 318 horsepower (322 metric horsepower), while the range-topping turbocharged example sees the light of day with a combined system output of 375 horsepower (380 metric horsepower). GM hasn’t revealed any pricing details either, but it will most likely happen closer to the launch date set for early 2027. While the Buick Electra GS PHEV will stay away from the U.S., it has every chance to make it to the European market. title: Buick Doesn’t Sell Sedans in the U.S., But China Will Get the Sleek New Electra GS Plug-In Hybrid - Car and Driver
content: Designed for the Chinese market, the Electra GS looks significantly different than the concept shown last year, with sharp, C-shaped LED headlights. While there are reports of a new sedan on the horizon, Buick’s lineup in the United States currently only consists of SUVs. But over in China, Buick offers a healthy arsenal of sedans, from the compact Verano to the larger LaCrosse. Now Buick is about to introduce a new electrified sedan called the Electra GS, and the first images of the new car have been leaked via China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). The MIIT periodically publishes information on upcoming automotive products, and the official filing is the first time we’ve seen the final production design for the Electra GS, which was first previewed by a concept in 2025. Confusingly, Buick already offers a sedan called the Electra L7 in China, sold with electric and range-extender plug-in hybrid powertrains, but the new Electra GS seems poised to be a less potent and more affordable option. The new Electra GS is a bit smaller than the Electra L7, measuring 196.0 inches from nose to tail, just over two inches shy of the L7. The GS is also 1.5 inches narrower and has a 5.3-inch shorter wheelbase than the L7. Under the hood, the Electra GS will employ a plug-in hybrid setup that uses either a 97-hp naturally aspirated 1.5-liter inline-four or a turbocharged 1.5-liter making 154 hp. The gas engines are paired with an electric motor producing 221 horsepower, which feeds off a lithium iron phosphate battery. Stylistically, the production Electra GS is a significant departure from the concept, with a more traditional sedan shape than the concept’s taller, hatchback look. The front end has thin headlights that wrap around a trim piece that stretches across the front and can be either body colored or finished in silver. The Electra GS has a fastback roofline and smooth surfacing, while the taillights span the width of the vehicle before curving inward. Overall, the Electra GS looks smart and modern, and Buick will hope that the GS can help reverse its sales slide in China. The Electra GS won’t be coming to the U.S., but it could give a sense of Buick’s future styling direction that could appear on the rumored gas-powered sedan expected to arrive in the next couple of years. Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan. title: How Aaru Uses Advanced AI Simulations to Predict Human Behavior - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Aaru, a two-and-a-half-year-old startup valued at $1 billion, is redefining market research and consumer intelligence by deploying multi-agent AI simulations to predict how humans will make decisions. Cam Fink, co-founder and CEO, and Ned Koh, co-founder and president, discuss Aaru's founding story and how advanced behavioral simulation overcomes the limitations of traditional consumer polling. In this conversation with Goldman Sachs Chief Information Officer Marco Argenti, they also explore the real-world enterprise applications of such predictive simulations across retail, financial services, and utilities, which are driving Aaru's rapid rise. Cam Fink:    We help you understand the composition of any population on the globe, and what decisions they make. What marketing campaigns they're going to click on, what subway lines they're going to ride. Ned Koh:      Our model is able to process how humans are able to think. Marco Argenti:      Welcome to Talks at GS. And also welcome to Ned and Cam from Aaru. Nowadays with AI almost like anything is possible, including being 19 and then, you know, having a $1 billion valuation startup, which is pretty incredible. So, since then, Aaru has become one of the most closely watched companies in the research and intelligence space. Thank you for being here. Cam Fink:    Thank you, Marco, for hosting us. We're really glad to have the opportunity today to talk a bit more about what we do. Marco Argenti:      The first question I'm going to ask you is, when was the first time you kind of realized that AI was something big? Cam Fink:    So, it's interesting you ask this because the ChatGPT moment was right in our senior year of high school. So, I remember, you know, having worked in the NLP space, in the computer vision space, where Ned and I were researchers before ChatGPT was released. You could tell that like AI was gaining a lot of capabilities very quickly. But it wasn't until it became actually productized into something consumers could use that all of a sudden it felt like not only was AI going to gain capabilities, but actually that it would create serious change in how people work on, you know, ideas, on products. But even still, like I remember the most enterprising students were already using AI to evaluate their answers to papers or come up with new ideas or test new things. And if you were even more enterprising before that, you would have been using the GPT-3 API to try and finish papers. So, you know, I think that was truly the moment that it became clear AI was going to be inevitable. Marco Argenti:      Was there another ah-ha moment recently? Because, you know, right now it feels like things are changing so fast. What's another inflection point that you've seen? Ned Koh:      The tools are incredibly powerful for being used for incredibly rudimentary application: note taking, you know, or summarization as like the key use cases or demonstrations of like how this can help you. And I still think in many businesses it is. It's easy to get behind. There's not really any friction to adopting those technologies. And so, I think that the larger change is this wave of product-first AI businesses. You saw that in health care. You saw that in, you know, financial services and beyond. But I think it was when it went beyond just those into more complex applications, for sure. Marco Argenti:      So, rolling back, like, kind of two basics. If you're in front of a CEO that doesn't know what Aaru is and you have a few seconds to explain, what would you say to them? What's your pitch? Like you're 30 second pitch. Cam Fink:    We predict human behavior. So, we help you understand the composition of any population on the globe and what decisions they make. We can help you understand how U.S. household purchase decision makers are going to purchase products, what marketing campaigns they're going to click on, what music they're going to stream, what subway lines they're going to ride. That's really the core of what we do: predicting behavior to make better business decisions. Marco Argenti:      And I think we met maybe two years ago for the first time. So, really early on. So, what have you learned in terms of sort of what kinds of decisions is AI really good at predicting and what others are not that good? Ned Koh:      Yeah, I think the first place that you look when you define what good means is understanding like the relative for how people make those decisions today. Right? So, let's take something that's like very simple - product launches. So, you have someone who's going in front of a survey, you're asking people questions. It's easy to benchmark. And that's a very interesting market. Product innovation is massive for us. But when you think about like use cases and how that's kind of diverged across the board, the most relevant ones for us and where we offer the most amount of value, of course, are places where you may not traditionally have data. Right? And so, that may exist in a population who doesn't respond to surveys. The example I like to give is like everybody in this room is wearing a shirt. Did anyone tell someone how much they were willing to pay for it? Probably not. Right? But then you get into like other categories. Right. You know this answer better than I do. But you know, there are four industries that make up about like 15% of the GDP of the U.S. Airlines, telecom, utilities, insurance. What are the times that matter to those companies about their behavior? When do you remember who your cell provider is? When your cell service goes out. When do you remember that you pay bills to Con Ed? When your power goes out. When do you remember that you fly a specific airline versus another? When your flight gets delayed. Right? And so, on and so forth. When do you remember who your insurance is? When you crash a car. And so, those businesses, despite being massive, the most important place and time for them to understand the behavior of their customers is somewhere where it's fundamentally impossible to get inside their head inside that moment. Right? And so, the most interesting use cases to us have always been those areas that have the most challenging to reach groups. The time frames of traditional research, it can take weeks and weeks or months to get people in a room and ask them questions or show them a product. You don't have the ability to do that. Right? So, things that are compressed in timeline are the use cases that are most relevant for simulation because human insight just doesn't reach that same level. Marco Argenti:      But why can't you just ask ChatGPT? Cam Fink:    Language models themselves alone can't understand human behavior with the depth and the capability that is required to actually allow a business to trust their decisions. There are a lot of startups out there now doing what you might call synthetic personas. That's sort of like the last generation of the technology we build. They can be useful. Those startups can help you get like a really quick read on marketing copy. But if you want a decision that you can trust, you need something that's grounded in real world outcomes. And that's where someone like Aaru would come in. Everything we do is AI. Right? So, what underpins our capabilities to predict human behavior are models. Models that we train. Models that leverage LLMs but aren't LLMs alone. But through fusing kind of LLMs with statistical models and traditional mathematical models, we're able to be far more accurate and take advantage of all of LLMs’ advantages without falling into those kind of gaps with LLMs and predicting behavior. Marco Argenti:      And how do you verify the accuracy and the results? I mean, what is what's ground truth for you guys? Ned Koh:      At the end of the day, if you're trying to predict and make a decision better, what you should be aiming for is a better business outcome. That was very first principle to us, right? You want to benchmark it to the sales result, to the product selling better or selling worse or the limited time offer not flying off the shelves like you wanted it to. The way that we've been able to grow our business so quickly is by making sure that people walk out of a pilot with us and don't just say, "Yes, we came to a decision faster," but rather we came to a decision better than we otherwise would have. Marco Argenti:      So, let's actually kind of bring it to life a little bit with some examples. What does the client actually get? Give us some examples of that. Cam Fink:    So, we do a lot of work with CPG companies. We do a lot of work with retail, beauty, apparel, kind of like anything that touches a consumer brand. And every kind of business ultimately sells a product. But for consumer brands, it's typically really linear. You can hold the product in your hand, right? A canned beverage, a carton of milk, whatever it might be. So, we do a lot of product innovation work where we'll go work with, you know, a canned sparkling water company, for example. And that sparkling water company will come to us and say, "Hey, we've built this great business around this one core product. What is our next new product line, right? Is it still hydration? Is it a shelf-stable dairy product? Is it an energy drink? Is it--," you know, all of these things. And we can use Aaru to do everything from the very core conceptual stage of what is the next frontier, right, all the way into figuring out who exactly is the purchasing audience. Then into the product concept itself specifically. So, say we pick out that it's an energy drink. We figure out who the energy drink purchaser is going to be from this brand. And then we figure out, okay, what flavors of energy drink do we want to put out in the world? And then we can do everything from getting as niche as optimizing the caffeine content to helping figure out the right pack size and carry that entire product innovation cycle from start to finish in just a few weeks. And one of our clients we worked with, their product innovation cycle traditionally was nine months long, right? That's actually pretty quick for the CPG industry. A lot of the big global companies might be taking 12 months, 18 months, to go from product idea or, you know, new market entrant to ready for manufacturing. We managed to squeeze it down into eight weeks. That was a really, really, really powerful case study. And now the product ended up hitting the shelves earlier this year. And they saw more success than they had with any of their previous product launches before. Marco Argenti:      And if I remember, that you guys can decide the size of the core. Tell us a little bit about that spectrum. Cam Fink:    Yeah, we don't go down to individual-by-individual level, right? We're never processing PII or any kind of individual data. So, we can't recreate Tom Smith from Iowa or Cameron Fink from New York City, right? We can get down to audiences that in the real world might only be a couple hundred people. I remember at one point doing hospitals that have to purchase this third-party risk management software. You're probably talking only a few hundred to low thousands of people nationwide. And yet we were still able to recreate that audience. And for the company that we did do that study for, they saw a massive impact from the work we could do together. So, we're getting really niche. We can talk about very small groups of buyers or social media influencers or Gen Z in one particular city metro. And then we can go as wide as US household purchase decision-makers or British residents or, you know, even residents of the EU if you want it. Marco Argenti:      And where do you get your data? Cam Fink:    I mean, it's a massive wealth of data sources, right? So, when we talk about how we leverage that data, we have audience data and we have behavioral outcomes data. On the audience data component, that's what helps us understand who actually exists inside of a population. So, when you come to me and you say, "Hey, I want to talk to ultra high net worth individuals in, you know, the United States and Canada," we can actually tell you what the distribution of that population looks like. And then we have behavioral outcome data. That helps us figure out what decisions are they going to make. So, that would, you know, be for each of these given value propositions, how will UHMW individuals react to them? Now, when it comes to where that data actually comes from, you can think about three different buckets for each of the data sources that we leverage. The first would be publicly accessible data. We're leveraging tons of things like the census, academic research where there's license to train on top of it, you know, anything else available publicly that our model is able to use. Then there's a lot of data we purchase. So, we buy data from everyone from credit card, you know, purchase history data providers to receipts, there are music streams, social media data. And then I would say really the final component is proprietary partnerships that we leverage. So, we do a lot of work with organizations that wouldn't fit the shape of traditional customers of ours but still want access to the impact of our software. We have done data sharing through those sorts of engagements before that's been incredibly powerful for what we do too. Marco Argenti:      How do you make your clients comfortable that they can share their most valuable data? Cam Fink:    Every client is sandboxed entirely. We're SOC 2 compliant. I didn't expect that I'd be saying that up on stage. But just in case anyone was worried, we have any InfoSec people in the room, we are SOC 2 compliant. We have all the compliance certifications we can. Most importantly, we do not train on customer data. And all of our clients are sandboxed. So, we actually end up being trusted as one of the most secure places to store, you know, that data because you would never be able to leverage a traditional research provider for anything sensitive. Right? You wouldn't want to go survey people and then someone takes a screenshot and says, "Hey, you know, my favorite brand was polling me about this on the internet." Instead, when you're leveraging our software, it's kept entirely secure to, you know, the model that we train. Marco Argenti:      You just said the models that we train. So, has your attitude and approach shifted over the years with regards to kind of using your own models versus using frontier models versus using quasi frontier open-source models? Cam Fink:    Yeah, our approach has definitely changed. I mean, when we started the business, we were definitely more in this realm of like, hey, can you take an LLM and train it on top of survey results? We found some of our own issues with that, right? Historically, we found it wasn't extensible. And that's what really led us to the next generation of our technology. So, those are all the models that we built ourselves. And that was really the big leap forward in terms of how our technology was able to reach the accuracy level that it is today. And so, we've been on, you know, all of our own models ever since that point in time. LLMs help us write analysis. They help us do tons of tasks as part of the simulation pipeline. But LLMs aren't driving the fundamental underlying prediction and behavior themselves. Now, when it comes to the LLMs we integrate, we use tons of different providers. We default to whatever is the best provider for each task that we have to do. Marco Argenti:      Which could be, you know, somehow maybe filtering all the data or explaining or prompt interpretation. But then the actual prediction machine or the simulation machine is your own. And that's your secret sauce. Ned Koh:      That is the secret sauce. Every single economist in the history of like behavioral science and everything else that you can go into has dreamed to be able to build a model off of something that's based on outcomes. You want to be able to remove as much bias as possible. Right? And so, not always is the magic and the data exclusively. It's much more in how our model is able to process things that are in many ways useless by their own right into something that can become a holistic view of how humans are able to think. Marco Argenti:      If every customer is protected and everything, how do you evolve the model? Cam Fink:    We're integrating new data sources all the time, right? So, the data that we have alone is enough that we are able to go out and make tons of valuable predictions. We can generate a lot of insight without having to integrate client data. Integrating client data for us is the key to unlock, you know, much deeper capabilities and integrations, both in terms of, you know, the simulation component and also in terms of how simulation results end up getting used. Marco Argenti:      I get that. But within, let's say, client engagement though, let's say we use it in private wealth in GS and then we want to kind of continue to learn, so do you allow your clients to continuously learn on the model that you provide and that stays theirs? Cam Fink:    It's actually interesting. A huge part of what we're talking about now is this idea of compounding intelligence. One of the biggest issues that our clients feel, one of their biggest pains, is this idea that traditional insight is very static, right? You run one survey, you run another survey, maybe you run a quarterly brand tracker, but it's not like those survey results are propelling forth the next survey that you run. And when you think about simulation, what's really incredible about the difference with our platform is that it's not just the power to like access more accurate, faster results. Our simulations can also contain the insights from all the simulations before it. And what that means is that it actually builds and compounds in value over time. You can imagine someone using our platform at the end of running nine projects about studying the Gen Z audience together, could come to us and say, "What are the insights, you know, we didn't even know we had about the Gen Z audience?" And that can go into helping build the next product that people might be interested in. So, a big focus for us is that compounding intelligence piece. Marco Argenti:      Are you guys mostly focused on the US, or do you have a lot of international customers? Cam Fink:    Yeah, we're a totally global business in terms of what we support. So, when you think about the range of Aaru today, it's over 130 countries across the globe. All of the EU, all of North America, much of South Asia, Southeast Asia, you know, and beyond. In the future, we are actually planning international expansion starting soon. But today, the bulk of our customers are based in North America. Marco Argenti:      And so, on that note, so do you think you need to tune sort of your models by culture and by countries? Ned Koh:      I think one of the best markets that is super relevant for a lot of the biggest enterprises that we work with today is expansion into Germany is really interesting, right? I've seen this across customers of ours in consumer electronics. I've seen this across customers of ours in financial services, right? Like it really goes across so many areas. The amount of safety regulations that people care about in like South Florida versus in, you know, Central Germany are vastly different. I can tell you that, right? Like the reality is, you know, you talk about why do we train models within this time when you're actually in runtime? Why do we keep them updated? These sorts of elements. The news, the way they digest social media, the things that changed their environment is what we like to call it within a given sim. Absolutely do. The context of how you and I make decisions on today versus tomorrow, absolutely do change. Does my race change? No, that's not the most important part to measure. So, we absolutely have to do that and have to do it on a hyper localized basis. Marco Argenti:      What's your biggest bottleneck at this point? Cam Fink:    100% hiring. Like it's the best people in the world is the number one thing you need for any fast-growing business. And so, when we think about what is going to-- has defined the last six months, going to define the next six months, next six years of Aaru, it's all going to be about working with the best people in the world. Marco Argenti:      And what kind of people are you looking for? Cam Fink: The first thing that we evaluate for is raw capability. We do look for people who are the best in the world at something. Right? People who are truly excellent at the craft or at their craft, so to speak, and represent the pinnacle of understanding knowledge capability in a given area. That's something that every person wants. Right? I'm sure Goldman wants people who are the best in their craft as well. We also look for people who are really high slope. So, even if you're not the absolute best in the world at something today, do you have the potential to be that in the future? Can you learn quickly? Can you adapt is something that's really important to us as well. And then finally, we look for people who are real collaborators. Every time someone joins our team, it's not just about whether or not they themselves are a really, really brilliant individual. Tons of people who are super smart and, you know, would be lucky to work at any incredible business on the globe. We spend a lot of time focusing on who is exactly right for Aaru and the people who have much to teach our team, much to teach myself, but we also have much to teach them and they can be, you know, leverage, exponential or multiplicative leverage to the people around them. Ned Koh:      Most of our research team, right, you'll have people who are pure math backgrounds. You'll have people who have done Alzheimer's and dementia research, right, who are able to tie in these really interesting areas. On the other side, we've recently brought on the head of research and data science from Qualtrics, who was there for over 13 years. Right? It's like you need some of those incredibly experienced perspectives to understand how to solve these problems. But you also need very fresh ones to think outside of the box to be able to do it as well. It's all about a combination and a balance. Cam Fink:    I think what we believed was true when we started this business is still true for the most part. Right? Like, we've always believed in being open communicators. We've always believed internally in, you know, the power of learning from each other, the power of collaboration. I think those are all important things. We've always believed in wanting people who are excellent at their craft. When we started to think about it, it's that as a growing business, it's actually time to write that down for the first time and distill it into the things that matter most for us. And that is what led us to kind of starting to think more about culture and principles in the last few weeks than we had previously. Ned Koh:      To that point, a really interesting thing that we've been discussing, especially with some of the larger implications of being able to model behavior, is this idea of like trustworthiness of a model. There's a very big difference between being worthy of trust and being a trustworthy company. And we certainly try to stay on the prior, right? We define that as being worthy of trust to the people who work next to you, right? That you're going to do an incredible job. It's being worthy of trust of your investors. It's being worthy of trust of your customers. It's being worthy of trust of the world that you're using the technology for the biggest impacts you can. Ned Koh:      Thank you so much for having us, Marco. Marco Argenti:      Was great. And good luck. Thank you so much.
