title: US Market Pulse November 2026 - Goldman Sachs Asset Management
content: Global activity remains supported by solid corporate and household balance sheets, AI investment, and fiscal cushions, which offset the dampening effect of tighter monetary policy and higher commodity prices. We expect 2027 growth near 2.5% in the US, and above 1% in Europe and Japan. The FOMC has telegraphed a pace for potential rate hikes of every other meeting. We expect them to raise rates in December, but the move in March will be highly dependent on the data. If inflation continues to normalize, with impulses from energy and tariffs rolling off, we may see them hold at 4.0-4.25%; if pressures broaden, they may have to hike. We expect the ECB to deliver one more hike in December to a peak policy rate of 2.75%. In an election cycle, our focus is not on who wins but rather what a win may change. In the US, a divided government likely means gridlock and more of the same. Upcoming elections in Spain, France, and Italy put a spotlight on fiscal risk, with fractured parliaments less likely to address debt burdens. Government bond yields may stay elevated, as seen recently in French OATs. Source: Bloomberg, Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research, and Goldman Sachs Asset Management. As of October 30, 2026. Earnings growth has been exceptional in 2026, boosted by AI investment and higher energy prices. We expect this growth to decelerate in 2027, but to remain supportive of equities. Historically, markets can rally for years past peak earnings growth, though they do become more idiosyncratic. As the AI cycle continues, we would expect focus to be on value capture, quality revenues, and balance sheet strength. Higher rates have led to scrutiny around the funding requirements for AI capex, leading to greater dispersion and spread widening across the AI complex. We remain cautious on IG tech but see scope for some near-term reversal in HY given the scale of the recent selloff. Credit fundamentals are supportive and supply is expected to slow in Q4. Our base case is for energy prices to moderate as supply/demand normalizes and risk premium recedes. However, upside risk remains from possible re-escalation in the Middle East or a colder than expected winter. We also see upward pressure on metals such as copper, where demand from electrification, data centers, and energy security is facing constrained mine supply; and gold, where central bank demand remains robust. Global equities have been resilient this year as strong earnings have offset energy market shocks. We think this diversification can continue to deliver in 2027 as the main themes around AI, defense, and economic security remain intact. Investor concerns about the sustainability of these trades appear to be well priced, particularly in EM where multiples are now cheaper than they have been ~90% of the time for the last 20 years. The massive investment in AI infrastructure has powered outsized earnings growth in EM, and particularly among the three main hardware providers. However, we also see strong growth potential in the specialized supply chains around AI including chip inputs, testing, packaging, and distribution. Additionally, commodity and consumer themes continue to play out across other markets, driving broad based strength across EM that investors have not seen for decades—annualized EPS growth from 2005-2025 was just 3%. Source: Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research. As of October 30, 2026. DM refers to developed markets. Chart shows the year-to-date total return for different parts of the TOPIX, STOXX 600, and S&P 500 Indices. Returns in Japan and Europe have also been strong beneath the surface, with the median stock beating the median in the US. We believe Europe’s strength reflects the lack of concentration in tech and the broader beneficiaries of higher rates, infrastructure spend, and energy prices, plus higher dividend yields that may help smooth volatility. Meanwhile Japan has been the beneficiary of multiple major market themes, including AI investment, defense, and infrastructure spend, and domestic fiscal impulse. Source: Bloomberg and Goldman Sachs Asset Management. As of October 30, 2026. Chart shows the difference in returns between the top 50 stocks and the bottom 50 stocks on a rolling 12-month basis. Dispersion has picked up across global markets this year as disruption has amplified potential winners and losers, with the difference between top and bottom performers averaging ~500% in EM and ~250% in DM. In our view, active management is always important in EM, a universe of 1,165 companies across 24 countries where geographic, sector, and security selection can add value. But even in DM, the high median stock returns and low cross-stock correlations that we see today may offer strong alpha potential. title: GS Corp lifts Q3 profit 46% as lubricants, power drive gains in South Korea - Chosunbiz
content: The 3rd-quarter results of GS Group's holding company, GS Corp., showed a marked improvement from the same period last year. Revenue rose sharply in the lubricants and power generation businesses, lifting the holding company's overall performance. GS Corp. said on Nov. 5 that operating profit for the 3rd quarter rose 46.4% on-year to 1.2748 trillion won. Revenue increased 11.2% to 7.2706 trillion won, and net profit jumped 66.9% to 680.4 billion won. However, compared with the previous quarter, operating profit and net profit fell 25.8% and 39.9%, respectively. Revenue was down 1.9%. Cumulative results through the 3rd quarter were 21.526 trillion won in revenue, 4.2507 trillion won in operating profit, and 2.6391 trillion won in net profit. Compared with the same period last year, revenue increased 15.1%, operating profit rose 96.8%, and net profit climbed 235.1%. A GS official said, "Consolidation operating profit in the 3rd quarter decreased from the previous quarter due to inventory effects from lower oil prices and a weaker exchange rate, but it increased from a year earlier as strong refining margins were maintained." By institutional sector, the petrochemical unit remained in the red for a second straight quarter because it failed to fully pass higher naphtha costs through to product prices. In contrast, the lubricants unit posted a record performance as global supply disruptions persisted, and the power generation unit also improved on entering the seasonal peak and on higher SMP (system marginal price). A GS official said, "In the 4th quarter, external uncertainties such as oil price volatility stemming from the Middle East situation and the recent surge in crude shipping rates will continue," adding, "We will respond flexibly to changes in the market environment to sustain the trend of improving results." title: Princeton to honor Nobel laureates Frances Arnold ’79 and Mary Brunkow GS ’91 at Alumni Day 2027 - The Daily Princetonian
content: Princeton’s top alumni honors will go to Nobel laureates Frances Arnold ’79, an engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology, and Mary Brunkow GS ’91, a distinguished investigator at Seattle’s Institute for Systems Biology. Arnold will receive the Woodrow Wilson Award while Brunkow will be awarded the James Madison Medal at Alumni Day on Feb. 20, 2027. The Woodrow Wilson Award was established in 1956 and is named after Woodrow Wilson, Class of 1879, who served as Princeton’s president before becoming U.S. president. The award is given to an undergraduate alum whose work represents Wilson’s saying, “Princeton in the nation’s service.” The 2026 awardee was Smithsonian executive Kevin Gover ’78, and Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor ’76 won the award in 2014. Originally from Pittsburgh, Arnold studied mechanical and aerospace engineering at Princeton, graduating magna cum laude in 1979. Her father, William Howard Arnold GS ’55, was a nuclear physicist and Princeton alumnus. Arnold was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2018 for her research that pioneered the directed evolution of enzymes involving introducing random mutations to proteins over many generations to engineer ones with desired traits. The Arnold Lab at Caltech is centered on engineering biological systems through “directed evolution,” with applications in pharmaceuticals, consumer products, renewable fuels, and bioremediation. According to her Nobel Prize biography, Arnold was one of the few women in her mechanical and aerospace engineering classes at Princeton, and studied economics, foreign languages, and art history along with the math and physics required for engineering. Beginning in her junior year, Arnold studied at the Center for Energy and Environmental Studies, now known as the Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment, with a focus on sustainable energy, influenced by the energy crisis of the 1970s and mentors at Princeton who believed that energy research could lead to positive societal change. Arnold is also an inventor with over 60 U.S. patents, co-founding the company Gevo, which produces biofuel from fermented plant materials, and Provivi, which creates alternatives to pesticides. Arnold did not provide comment in time for publication. The James Madison Medal, named for Princeton’s first graduate alumnus, is the highest honor a graduate alum can receive. It is awarded to alumni who have exhibited extraordinary public service, furthered graduate education, or had exceptional career success. Previous awardees have included Terence Tao GS ’96, Julia Wolfe GS ’12, and Robert Kahn GS ’64. The medal is not Brunkow’s first major honor, who won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2025, alongside immunologists Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi for their work in peripheral immune tolerance. Brunkow said the medal was “a real honor” in an interview with The Daily Princetonian. “I see the list of all the past awardees, and it’s pretty amazing to be part of that esteemed crowd of achievers.” Brunkow earned her Ph.D. in molecular biology from Princeton in 1991. Her doctoral adviser was Shirley M. Tilghman, who would go on to serve as Princeton’s 19th president. Beyond helping her develop a strong foundation in scientific methodology and science communication, Brunkow also credits Tilghman as “an amazing role model.” “There weren’t very many really senior-level women in research at that time,” Brunkow told the ‘Prince.’ “I was lucky at the time to be … working with somebody who really embodied what it takes to succeed in a really difficult role.” Brunkow currently works at the Institute for Systems Biology in Seattle, where she serves as a Distinguished Investigator in the Hood Lab. Her involvement in biology has changed considerably throughout her career, ranging from genomics to her Nobel Prize-winning research in immunology. Today, her work centers on systems biology. When asked about what draws her to the field, she cited the potential impact her research can have. “[It is] very satisfying and very exciting to me that the science has evolved a lot over the last few decades so that we really can think about making discoveries that will really impact how clinicians treat patients,” she told the ‘Prince.’ Both Brunkow and Arnold will receive their awards on campus in the Spring.
